papers.title: Sex-dependent rewarding effects of nicotine in mice are prevented by the atypical antipsychotic aripiprazole
papers.abstract: Nicotine stands amongst the most commonly used drugs in contemporary societies. Preparations for nicotine consumption range from traditional tobacco products (smoking) to modern electronic cigarettes (vaping). However, its rewarding and reinforcing effects vary as a function of dose and biological sex. In addition, few treatments exists for nicotine use disorders Here we sought to characterize the effects of nicotine on anxiety in the elevated plus maze (EPM) and reward in the conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm in male and female mice and test the hypothesis that aripiprazole, a partial dopamine agonist, prevents nicotine-induced CPP. Nicotine effects were tested at 0.25, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg. The highest dose reduced basal locomotion in both males and females exposed to the open field and reduced open arm exploration in males in the EPM. Thus, the apparent anxiogenic-like effect is confounded by a reduction in basal exploratory activity. In the CPP paradigm, nicotine 0.5 mg/kg served as a reward conditioned stimulus in males, but not females. Finally, aripiprazole (0.1, 1 and 10 mg/kg) consistently prevented the acquisition of nicotine (0.5 mg/kg) CPP in males. These findings show a sexually dimorphic effect of nicotine in mice and suggest the antipsychotic aripiprazole as a potential pharmacological approach for reducing nicotine reward.

papers.title: Anthropogenic noise affects Oikopleura dioica behaviour in a life stage- and signal-dependent manner
papers.abstract: Anthropogenic noise is an increasingly important pollutant of marine environments, yet its effects on zooplankton remain poorly understood. The appendicularian Oikopleura dioica is a globally distributed filter-feeding tunicate whose locomotion and house-building behaviour directly influence feeding efficiency and carbon export. Here, we investigated how anthropogenic noise affects behaviour across the life cycle of O. dioica, from larvae to juveniles and adults, using stage-specific tracking and quantitative behavioural analyses to assess responses to a high-intensity standardized noise band (MSFD-NB) and a vessel-derived noise signal (Vessel-DNS). Animals exhibited consistent behavioural alterations during and after noise exposure, and the responses differed strongly among life stages and between noise signals. Larvae showed the greatest sensitivity, displaying increased locomotor activity and altered movement dynamics during exposure, as well as persistent post-exposure effects. Juveniles exhibited treatment-dependent changes in trajectory organization, whereas adults showed modifications in orientation, turning behaviour, and tail-driven propulsion. In adults residing within their filter-feeding house, noise altered pumping-associated movements without affecting house-expansion frequency. These findings demonstrate that anthropogenic noise impacts behaviour throughout the O. dioica life cycle in a stage- and signal-specific manner, suggesting that noise pollution may not only impact individual performance, but potentially also ecological processes linked to marine food webs, carbon sequestration, and consequently, ocean health.

papers.title: TCDD-Induced m⁶A Profiling Identifies SUV39H2 as a Positive Regulator of Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor Signaling
papers.abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) mediates cellular responses to environmental contaminants, including 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD). Although AHR-dependent transcriptional regulation is well characterized, the contributions of RNA modifications and chromatin-associated regulators to AHR signaling remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated TCDD-associated changes in N-methyladenosine (mA) RNA modification and identified suppressor of variegation 3-9 homolog 2 (SUV39H2) as a previously unrecognized positive regulator of AHR signaling. Exploratory methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq) and matched RNA-seq analyses were performed in vehicle- and TCDD-treated HepG2 cells, followed by independent molecular and functional validation. TCDD increased mA enrichment and mRNA stability of canonical AHR-responsive transcripts, including CYP1A1, CYP1A2, and AHRR, accompanied by increased gene expression. Notably, SUV39H2 was identified as a TCDD-responsive mA-enriched transcript exhibiting increased mRNA stability and protein expression without a substantial change in steady-state mRNA abundance. Functional studies demonstrated that SUV39H2 depletion and pharmacological inhibition attenuated TCDD-induced AHR target gene expression and transcriptional activity, whereas SUV39H2 overexpression enhanced AHR-dependent responses. CUT&RUN-qPCR analyses further implicated SUV39H2 in AHR-associated transcriptional regulation at the CYP1A1 enhancer. Consistent with the cellular findings, pharmacological inhibition of SUV39H2 attenuated TCDD-induced expression of AHR-responsive genes in mouse liver. Collectively, these findings identify SUV39H2 as a previously unrecognized positive regulator of AHR signaling and suggest that TCDD-associated mA modification and mRNA stabilization contribute to the regulation of AHR-responsive transcripts and chromatin-associated regulatory factors.

papers.title: Longitudinal computer vision-based behavioural phenotyping of group-housed dogs for translational and welfare research
papers.abstract: Continuous behavioural monitoring is essential for assessing animal welfare and individual behavioural variation, yet traditional observation-based methods are labour-intensive and prone to bias. Here, we developed a modular framework with computer vision for automated behavioural profiling of group-housed Beagles, integrating You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based models for pose estimation, individual identification, and enrichment detection. A ceiling-mounted infrared camera system enabled uninterrupted monitoring under standard kennel conditions. The identity-independent YOLO-POSE model achieved 99% precision, 97% recall, and an mAP50 of 0.98, while the YOLO classification model reached 95% accuracy for individual identification without external markers. Combining posture, identity, and environmental information enabled automated quantification of spatial use, locomotor activity, social interactions, corridor-oriented behaviour, drinking behaviour, and enrichment use. Overall, this framework captured distinct behavioural profiles of individual dogs from the same litter housed in the same kennel, which can be used to assess animal welfare and to evaluate environmental enrichments objectively. Together, we demonstrate a scalable and non-invasive approach for continuous individual behavioural profiling of group-housed dogs for computational ethology and translational research. By separating pose estimation from identity assignment, the framework enables flexible deployment across changing social groups and facilitates application to previously unseen individuals with minimal training.

papers.title: Daily-Academic: A Semantic Literature Discovery and Journal Tracking Platform for Biomedical Research
papers.abstract: Objective: Biomedical researchers monitoring newly published literature rely on fragmented combinations of keyword alerts, manual database searches, journal subscriptions and repository portals. We aimed to develop and evaluate an integrated platform that unifies semantic literature discovery, journal monitoring and linked omics dataset exploration within a single researcher-oriented workflow, driven by a user profile that remains explicit and editable. Methods: Daily-Academic aggregates publication metadata from biomedical literature repositories and public omics resources and encodes titles and abstracts as dense semantic representations to support similarity-based retrieval beyond keyword matching. Recommendations are ranked by combining semantic relevance to the user profile with publication recency and journal-level preferences. The profile is derived from three user-supplied signals: a free-text statement of research interests, an optional link to the user's own publication record, and interaction history. Retrieval quality was assessed on an offline benchmark of 30 biomedical queries over a fixed corpus of 259,246 publications, comparing Daily-Academic with a lexical BM25 baseline and a PubMedBERT bi-encoder under pooled assessment with graded relevance judgements. Results: [Insert the corrected figures once the re-annotation is complete: precision and nDCG at rank 10 for all three methods, and the outcome of the paired significance tests.] Query-level analysis indicated that the differences were distributed across queries rather than driven by a small subset. Conclusion: Integrating semantic retrieval into a unified discovery workflow with an inspectable user model improved the quality of top-ranked biomedical literature relative to established lexical and dense baselines. Because the benchmark is user-free, the adaptive component of personalisation was inactive and the ranking weights untuned; the observed advantage therefore reflects the semantic representation rather than adaptive personalisation. The platform is publicly available at https://www.daily-academic.com. Keywords: biomedical informatics, literature discovery, semantic retrieval, recommender systems, journal tracking, personalized feeds, scientific monitoring

papers.title: Evaluation of sources of variability in a TEER (trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance) system
papers.abstract: Trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements are a key nondestructive measurement of the barrier integrity of cells grown on inserts. To support the use of TEER measurements in bioassays, we have evaluated the sources of variability in a case study involving a chamber-based TEER system to assess a gut co-culture model. Data from 23 separate experiments, each lasting 22 d, were evaluated. Multiple lines of evidence suggested minimal variability within a run, a period during which several plates were analyzed sequentially. In contrast, run-to-run variability was substantially larger, even when two runs were performed several hours apart on the same day. Bayesian analysis of both KCl and blank insert data revealed that run-to-run variability was among the largest sources of variability, with relative uncertainty values of 3 % to 6 % of the mean value. Correlational analysis investigated whether deviations of KCl or blank insert TEER values within a run compared to long-term median values were correlated with deviations of the biculture gut model values within that same run from their long-term median values. Unexpectedly, the KCl values were not correlated, while the blank insert values had a weak correlation. We also evaluated the information gained from different control measurements. The findings from this study can influence how statistical analyses are performed on TEER results and can inform the design of robust TEER methods. For example, the approaches described here can be used to characterize variability within and among runs in TEER measurements for other methods.

papers.title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered Cas13b ribonucleoproteins targeting survivin overcome gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely due to its poor response to chemotherapy and the development of drug resistance. Survivin (BIRC5), an inhibitor of apoptosis frequently overexpressed in PDAC, contributes to tumor cell survival and gemcitabine resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for the delivery of preassembled spCas13b ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to achieve transient and sequence-specific RNA silencing in pancreatic cancer cells. We optimized ionizable lipid formulations for Cas13b RNP encapsulation and identified a formulation achieving approximately 80% encapsulation efficiency, with sustained colloidal stability and gene-silencing activity during seven days of storage at 4{degrees}C. LNP-delivered Cas13b RNPs efficiently silenced endogenous BIRC5 in three pancreatic cancer cell lines, reducing survivin protein levels and inducing apoptosis. In gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells, BIRC5 silencing synergistically enhanced the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine in vitro. This therapeutic combination was further evaluated in a PANC-1 xenograft model, where only the combined administration of BIRC5-targeting Cas13b RNP-LNPs and gemcitabine significantly inhibited tumor growth, without apparent systemic toxicity. Intratumoral administration also restricted nanoparticle distribution to the injected tumors. These findings establish LNP-mediated delivery of Cas13b RNPs as a new strategy for transient RNA-targeted therapy and provide proof of concept for combining survivin silencing by Cas13b with chemotherapy to address gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer.

papers.title: Diverging light-responsive behaviors in genetically similar strains of Hydra vulgaris
papers.abstract: Sensory perception drives behavior by bridging the external environment with internal states. The freshwater cnidarian Hydra vulgaris serves as a useful model for capturing these dynamics due to its structural simplicity and distinct, state-dependent behaviors. However, few studies examine behavioral differences between strains that may arise from distinct genetic backgrounds, and none have compared behaviors from closely related lines. Here, we compare the phototactic profiles of two independently derived F1 lines created by self-crossing the standard laboratory AEP line: Hydra vulgaris AEP Irvine and AEP Kiel. While satiety alters behavior in both lines, starved AEP Irvine animals display stochastic wandering rather than the robust positive phototaxis seen in the AEP Kiel strain. A biased-correlated random walk model reproduces both behaviors by modifying jump rate and head angle. Despite lacking directional phototaxis, AEP Irvine remains light-sensitive: in darkness, animals exhibit fewer jumps, greater jump distance, and longer head-angle persistence. Behavioral motif classification reveals that light exposure alters time spent in stillness and elongation, as well as a few transition probabilities. These findings highlight behavioral differences between Hydra strains derived from the same parental line, providing an opportunity to identify molecular and genetic mechanisms coupling photoreception to state-dependent directional navigation.

papers.title: Actinium-225 Pretargeted Radioimmunotherapy against Colorectal Cancer using Self-Assembling and Disassembling Antibodies
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide. GPA33, expressed on 95% of CRC, has been extensively targeted by IgG-attached payloads in conventional radioimmunotherapy (RIT), but toxicity was dose-limiting. A 2-step pretargeted radioimmunotherapy (PRIT) regimen using Self-Assembling-Disassembling antibody (SADA) specific for GPA33 (10 mg/kg) intravenous (IV) in step #1 and 24 h later [86Y]Y-ABD (9 nmole) IV in step #2, avoided normal gut uptake in non-human primates. Dosimetry results based on tissue counting in murine models using GPA33-SADA IV in step #1 and [225Ac]Ac-Pr in step #2, were 30.88, 0.1 and 2.56 Gy/uCi (Gy/37 kBq; RBE= 1), respectively for subcutaneous (sq) SW1222 tumor, blood and kidney, demonstrating favorable therapeutic ratios (309 for blood; 12 for kidney). Established sq SW1222 xenografts treated with 225Ac-SADA-PRIT showed dose dependent improvement in median survival (MS). Using one cycle of 2 doses 7 days apart (74kBq + 74kBq of 225Ac), majority of mice had complete tumor volumetric responses of sq SW1222, LS174T, LOVO and intraperitoneal SW1222 xenografts. Complete response was confirmed histologically at 180 days, accompanied by statistically significant improvements in MS. All treatments were well tolerated, with transient reversible weight loss (<15%), minimal hematologic, and no acute (within 30 days post 225Ac) chemical toxicities. At necropsy, kidneys showed minimal to marked subclinical tubular injury. The ability of a single cycle of 225Ac-SADA-PRIT to induce major CRC response and durable remission with minimal acute toxicities in multiple xenograft models while avoiding on-target off-tumor gut toxicity is encouraging, although subclinical histologic renal and ovarian damage remain a concern.

papers.title: Mitragynine reduces symptoms of alcohol use disorder (and tinnitus) in a self-medication of rodents
papers.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major psychiatric disease. Available pharmacotherapies show rather modest compliance and efficacy. Tinnitus is a highly aversive hearing problem, that may arise from the same unsolved problems as AUD. Based on a patient report of Kratom, a Southeast Asian plant preparation, efficacy in the self-medication of AUD and tinnitus, we tested the main active Kratom alkaloid, mitragynine, for its therapeutic action in AUD mouse models covering various symptoms of the disease. We found that experimenter administered mitragynine (i.p.) inhibits well-established ongoing alcohol consumption in a social setting when alcohol is permanently available. Mitragynine also inhibits alcohol consumption in a non-social, isolated setting. While mitragynine did not work for prophylaxis during abstinence, it markedly attenuated the relapse to binge drinking with alcohol availability restricted to a limited time. Furthermore, mitragynine reduced alcohol seeking behaviour during its establishment as well as during retrieval from memory. It was also effective to attenuate its re-establishment after extinction. We found significant antidepressive effects of mitragynine, during alcohol withdrawal. To address the compliance problem for pharmacotherapies, we established a test that can monitor this and found that mice after a short training, learned to orally self-administer mitragynine hydrochloride leading to a strong reduction in voluntary alcohol drinking. In parallel, mitragynine reduced tinnitus after a noise trauma in a gerbil model. Together, these findings suggest that mitragynine may be used as a pharmacotherapy for AUD and tinnitus with an expected high compliance rate.

papers.title: Social compensation changes predicted effects of individual loss in animal societies
papers.abstract: Animal populations globally are suffering significant declines; many species are social, and individuals are likely to adjust their social behaviour as they lose associates. Therefore, social networks may respond to population decline as individuals adjust their social connections in response to changing social environments. Our understanding of how individual responses to loss of their associates alters the structure of their social networks is rudimentary. To quantify how social responses to individual loss can alter network structure, we simulated individual loss and compensatory formation of new social ties across 268 empirical animal social networks. Compensation changed the structural effects of individual loss, though these effects often depended on which individuals were removed. Loss of central, peripheral or random individuals produced different network responses, while social compensation had similar effects regardless of compensation strategy. Together, these results suggest that compensatory social behaviour can reorganise social networks as populations decline, even if departing from the original structure. Accounting for these responses may improve predictions of how demographic change affects social structure, particularly when losses are socially patterned and without knowing the compensation strategy. Broadly, our findings highlight compensation as a potentially important process linking individual social behaviour to the reorganisation of animal societies.

papers.title: LUC3D: Multi-animal 3D pose tracking in the browser
papers.abstract: Animal behavior unfolds in three dimensions over time, yet accessible scientific tools for analyzing it in its natural form remain limited. Uncertainty from popular 2D pose methods can be refined with multi-camera approaches to produce more accurate 3D estimates. This paper presents LUC3D (Label Unification and Correspondence in 3D Annotation GUI), a browser-based 3D GUI for reducing the amount of manual labor required for labeling, proofreading, and multi-camera multi-animal tracking while requiring no installation to maximize accessibility. As proof-of-concept we present two datasets of proofread multi-camera 3D triangulated pose data of mouse social behavior, a protocol for generating 3D consistent labels, and a cross-view re-identification tracking algorithm for multi-animal multi-camera pose data. This tool allows for the widespread adoption of 3D pose estimation techniques for studying social behavior while reducing the cost of entry for neuroscience labs across the world.

papers.title: Trunk stiffness of the American giant millipede during terrain bridging
papers.abstract: Slender, flexible bodies allow animals such as millipedes to regularly traverse heterogeneous, uneven terrain and complex obstacles by using their body's compliance to conform to the terrain. Orchestrating a slender body's many degrees of freedom poses a control challenge, with possible strategies ranging in complexity and cost, from complex muscle actuation patterns to simple passive compliance. Here we investigate these behavioral strategies by examining American giant millipedes (Narceus americanus) bridging between terrains of different heights. We model millipede trunk mechanics using Cosserat rods and compare resulting equilibrium configurations with experimental data to determine bending stiffnesses that best recreates their posture and test for regional and temporal variations. We find that a highly compliant, passive rod best captures millipede poses during periods where its middle section is unsupported. This supports the hypothesis that millipedes do not strongly actively stiffen their trunk during terrain bridging, relying instead on their body's passive compliance.

papers.title: Making monkeys of caregivers: Evaluating the use of caregiver behaviour as social enrichment for lab-housed Rhesus and Cynomolgus Macaques
papers.abstract: Enrichment is pivotal to captive animal welfare. Social enrichment is of particular importance for social animals who, due to laboratory space or protocols, are not housed in larger groups. The objective of our study was to see if caregivers could act as an additional source of social enrichment to pair-housed research macaques. 5 adult Rhesus (Macaca Mulatta) and 3 adult Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) were enrolled in the study. Every day, for 3 weeks, caregivers would spend 6 minutes interacting with the monkeys during afternoon feeding. Half the monkeys received human behaviour (HB), where the caregivers interacted with the monkeys using human body language and speaking softly. The other half received monkey-like behaviour (MB), in which caregivers would attempt to imitate monkey behaviour, all the while avoiding eye-contact or speaking (both of which may be perceived as aggressive). Our results showed that monkeys were more likely to engage in interactions before feeding, indicating that this may be an ideal time to provide social enrichment. Monkeys from both groups showed a 3.5 {+/-} 1.5 (F54 = 3.34, p = 0.058) decrease in the frequency of cage-directed abnormal behaviours and a 1.2 {+/-} 0.53 (F54 = 2.78, p = 0.067) decrease in the frequency of stereotypic abnormal over the course of the experiment. In addition, all monkeys saw a 12.9 {+/-} 6.1% (F54 = 2.40, p = 0.010) increase in the proportion of time spent interacting positively with cage-mates, including a 10.6 {+/-} 4.78% (F54.1 = 2.47, p = 0.077) increase in time spent grooming. This research contributes to the enhancement of animal care by helping to establish evidence-based guidelines for the proper care of non-human primates in research. It further deepens our understanding of social enrichment provided by humans as a cost-effective way of managing boredom.

papers.title: Morphological Changes and Mechanistic Analysis in Osteoblasts Induced by Long-Term Exposure to Radioactive Strontium
papers.abstract: Radioactive strontium-89 (89Sr) is preferentially deposited in bone tissue, where it directly interacts with osteoblasts; however, the morphological and molecular consequences of sustained 89Sr exposure remain poorly characterized. In this study, mouse pre-osteoblast MC3T3-E1 cells were induced to differentiate into osteoblasts and continuously exposed to 3.7 x 103 Bq/mL 89Sr for nine consecutive passages. Morphological alterations were monitored throughout the exposure period, and the cells were subjected to RNA transcriptomic sequencing, non-targeted GC/MS-based metabolomics, and non-targeted LC/MS-based lipidomics, followed by integrative bioinformatics analysis. Prolonged 89Srr exposure markedly enlarged the cell nuclei and increased the number of intracellular vesicles in osteoblasts. Multi-omics co-enrichment analysis revealed metabolic perturbations centered on the "choline metabolism in cancer" and "fat digestion and absorption" pathways, while upregulated genes--including Hif1a, Egfr, Pdgfb, Egf, and Pdgfd--constituted key interaction modules underlying these alterations. Collectively, these findings suggest that 89Sr toxicity may be mediated through co-enriched pathways centered on choline metabolism and lipid digestion and absorption, driven by the upregulation of hub interaction modules comprising Hif1a, Egfr, Pdgfb, Egf, and Pdgfd. This study provides novel theoretical evidence for the toxicological mechanisms of radioactive strontium.

papers.title: The impact of tail-cup handling as an alternative method for picking up laboratory mice
papers.abstract: The way that laboratory rodents are handled has a significant impact on their welfare. Picking up mice by the tail increases anxiety, reduces voluntary interaction with handlers, and reduces behavioural test reliability compared to more refined handling methods, such as picking up mice inside a handling tunnel or cupping freely on the hand. An alternative in use by the community is to restrain a mouse by the tail-base while scooping it up on the hand and supporting its weight (tail-cup method). Here, we assess whether tail-cup handling is a welfare refinement compared to picking up mice by tail or tunnel, using both sexes of two strains (BALB/c, C57BL/6). Tail-cup handling reduced aversion to interact with the handler compared to tail handling, but to a much smaller extent than tunnel handling. Tail-cup and tunnel handling both reduced anxiety in an elevated plus maze relative to tail-handled mice. However, test reliability was substantially better using tunnel handling in a habituation-dishabituation task, greatly reducing numbers of animals required for testing. These findings generalised across sexes and strains tested. While tail-cup handling provides some improvement over traditional tail handling, tunnel handling appears to be more beneficial for mouse welfare and behavioural reliability.

papers.title: 'Silent Spring' revisited: sublethal neonicotinoid exposure suppresses birdsong
papers.abstract: Neonicotinoids are widely used pesticides linked to impaired reproduction and population decline in birds. However, the behavioral mechanisms connecting exposure to reduced reproduction remain unclear. Here, we examined the effects of imidacloprid, one of the most commonly used neonicotinoids, on singing in male zebra finches. Birds received sublethal doses of imidacloprid through drinking water over 30 days, followed by a 30-day washout. Using continuous acoustic monitoring and female-presentation assays, we quantified non-courtship and female-directed courtship song and assessed body mass, locomotion, non-vocal displays, and song structure. During the 30-day drinking-water exposure, imidacloprid reduced daily non-courtship singing, with effects persisting into washout. It also reduced courtship song, whereas body mass, locomotion, non-vocal displays, and song structure showed no detectable treatment-related changes. In a separate experiment, acute imidacloprid injection also reduced courtship song but was accompanied by some non-vocal behavioral impairment. These findings identify song output as a sensitive behavioral endpoint for neonicotinoid toxicity, suggesting that even low doses might impair songbird reproduction by suppressing singing before conventional signs of toxicity become apparent. This suppression of song production implies that widespread neonicotinoid use could silently contribute to population declines in wild birds by compromising their ability to attract mates, defend territories, form pair bonds, and successfully breed. Song output may therefore complement conventional measures when assessing the sublethal effects of neonicotinoids in songbirds.

papers.title: Tissue-specific biotransformation shapes the toxicity of 6PPD-quinone in fish cell models
papers.abstract: Acute mortality of salmonids exposed to urban runoff has been linked to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), a transformation product of the widely used tire antiozonant 6PPD. However, the cellular processes underlying 6PPD-Q toxicity remain poorly understood. Beyond the well-documented differences in species sensitivity, here we determined tissue-specific responses in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) cell lines exposed to 6PPD-Q: brain-derived cells (RTBrain) were more sensitive than gill-derived cells (RTgill-W1). To unravel the cellular mechanisms underlying such differential responses, we combined time-resolved 6PPD-Q cellular depletion kinetics, targeted biotransformation product (BTP) profiling, transporter inhibition experiments, and cytotoxicity assessments. Both cell models biotransformed 6PPD-Q, but RTBrain displayed a 6.6-fold higher cellular clearance rate than RTgill-W1. Chemical profiling identified four BTPs, including para-aryl-OH-6PPD-Q, which was selectively toxic to RTBrain but not RTgill-W1 cells. These findings reveal tissue-specific toxicokinetics as potential determinants of differential 6PPD-Q toxicity even within the same species. More broadly, this integrated approach highlights the importance of considering biotransformation and the production of biologically active transformation products when assessing susceptibility to emerging contaminants.

papers.title: Impact of culture medium on linezolid PK/PD activity against Staphylococcus aureus in a Hollow-Fiber infection model simulating cerebrospinal fluid exposure
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess the impact of the culture medium on the effect of linezolid against Staphylococcus aureus using Time-Kill curves (TKC) and Hollow-Fiber infection model (HFIM) by reproducing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) PK profiles. TKC were performed over 30 h in Mueller-Hinton Broth (MHB), artificial CSF (aCSF) and human CSF (hCSF) at 0, 0.25, 1, 4 x linezolid MIC. Clinical CSF concentrations after 600 or 900 mg q12h and 900 mg q8h were reproduced in HFIM over 96 h in MHB and aCSF. A PK/PD model developed from MHB TKC and HFIM data was combined with hCSF TKC data to predict bacterial counts in HFIM in hCSF. In TKC, bacterial growth was slower in hCSF than MHB. Linezolid was bactericidal in MHB, but only bacteriostatic in hCSF. In aCSF, no growth and no decrease in bacterial counts was observed. In HFIM, bacterial growth was predicted to be also slower in hCSF than MHB. Linezolid at 900 mg q8h was needed to obtain a bactericidal effect in MHB, while 600 mg q12h would be sufficient in hCSF. Despite aCSF renewal in HFIM, no growth and no impact of the treatment was observed whatever linezolid dosing regimen. Bacterial growth and linezolid effect differed between media. MHB overestimated bacterial growth and suggested higher dosing regimen than hCSF, questioning its suitability for central nervous system infections in vitro studies. Using aCSF would be a promising alternative, although its composition requires optimisation to better reproduce bacterial growth and linezolid effect observed in hCSF.

papers.title: Pharmacolibrary: Interoperable executable models for PK, PD and PGx derived from published evidence
papers.abstract: Published pharmacological knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous scientific literature, databases, and computational models, making systematic reuse, comparison, and reproducibility difficult. We present Pharmacolibrary v26.11, a source-traceable resource that connects pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and pharmacogenomic (PGx) knowledge with executable models, simulations, and interactive visualizations. A multi-agent workflow combines LLM-assisted literature retrieval and extraction with deterministic validation, ontology mapping, provenance tracking, automated model generation, and rule-based review. The system transforms published evidence and extracted parameters into executable models across Modelica, FMI, SBML, MATLAB, and CellML and provides browser-based simulations for research and education. Preliminary evaluation indicates that decomposing literature extraction into multiple stages improves parameter recovery compared with single-pass extraction and that locally deployed open-weight models can provide performance that is at least comparable with frontier commercial LLMs. Pharmacolibrary provides a foundation for scalable, auditable curation of pharmacological knowledge and for connecting published evidence to reusable computational models across research, simulation, and education.

papers.title: Native-like 3D colonoids reveal mechanisms of colonic drug disposition
papers.abstract: Intestinal organoid research in drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADME-T) has focused predominantly on small intestinal enteroids, leaving colonic drug handling comparatively unexplored. Here, we established and characterized adult colonic stem cell-based three-dimensional (3D) organoid (colonoid) models as physiologically relevant New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). Donor-matched mucosal tissue, isolated primary epithelial cells, and 3D colonoids were characterized using global and targeted proteomics, fixed and live-cell microscopy, functional ADME-T assays and targeted lipidomics. This complementary analysis identified isolated primary epithelial cells as a more representative native epithelial reference than excised mucosal tissue. Suspended differentiated apical- and basal-out colonoid configurations more closely matched this reference across the assessed characteristics. Together, these two configurations provided access to both apical and basolateral epithelial surfaces, enabling functional studies of key drug transporters (P-gp, BCRP) and metabolizing enzymes (CYP3A4, UGT1A, SULT1A) in a native-like setting. Measurement of intracellular bioavailability (Fic), reflecting drug availability to intracellular targets, revealed lipophilicity-dependent microvillar absorption mechanisms. Hydrophilic compounds exploited the enlarged membrane surface provided by microvilli, whereas highly permeable lipophilic compounds seemingly entered only at the microvillus tips. Compared with HEK293 cells, an established reference model for Fic measurements, colonoids combined native-like epithelial geometry with higher phospholipid content and generally stronger intracellular drug binding, highlighting the importance of both architecture and cellular composition for studying colonic drug disposition. These colonoid models provide a physiologically relevant platform for investigating colonic ADME-T and reveal how microvillar architecture shapes intracellular drug bioavailability.

papers.title: Individual variation in emergence behaviour and responses to sound exposure in zebrafish
papers.abstract: Fish respond to sound through behavioural changes, but whether these responses are associated with individual differences in emergence behaviour remains unclear. We examined emergence behaviour across two successive tests and its association with immediate responses to sound in 112 adult zebrafish (Danio rerio). Emergence latency was used to classify fish as bold, intermediate, or shy. Latency to enter the upper half of the aquarium was measured before treatment onset, while vertical midline crossings were quantified during 20-s windows immediately before and after sound or ambient-treatment onset. Emergence latency decreased significantly in the second test, and individual latencies were weakly positively correlated across tests. Upper-half latency did not differ significantly between bold and shy fish. Changes in midline crossings differed significantly between treatments, with a greater reduction under sound exposure than under ambient conditions. Exploratory analyses provided insufficient evidence that the association between emergence latency and changes in crossings differed between treatments for either emergence test. These findings demonstrate individual variation and changes in emergence behaviour across successive assessments, alongside an immediate effect of sound on vertical movement. However, they do not establish stable personality differences or emergence latency as a predictor of sound-specific behavioural responses.

papers.title: Striking Differences in Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) Deconjugation by Human Fecal Microbiota: The Pilot-10 Human Donor Study
papers.abstract: Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) is a widely used brominated flame retardant with multiple adverse health effects. Although TBBPA undergoes phase II conjugation to facilitate elimination, gut microbial deconjugation may regenerate unconjugated TBBPA, increasing intestinal re-exposure. However, the extent of interindividual variability and its underlying microbial determinants remain poorly understood. To address this critical knowledge gap, we hypothesized that human fecal microbiota exhibit donor-dependent differences in TBBPA-sulfate (S-TBBPA) deconjugation and potential downstream debromination to tribromobisphenol A (Tri-BBPA). In our Pilot-10 Human Donor Study (PM10), fecal microbiota from five healthy adult male and five female human donors were incubated anaerobically with S-TBBPA at 37 C for six hours. Heat-inactivated microbiota served as controls. S-TBBPA, unconjugated TBBPA, and Tri-BBPA were quantified using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Metagenomic shotgun sequencing (MGS) was performed followed by microbial taxonomic and gene-family profiling using MetaPhlAn v4.11 and HUMAnN v3.9, respectively. Unheated fecal microbiota from all donors regenerated TBBPA, whereas heat inactivation nearly abolished its formation, supporting microbial enzyme-dependent deconjugation of S-TBBPA. The proportion of regenerated TBBPA varied substantially among donors, accounting for approximately 10-50% of the combined detected S-TBBPA and TBBPA. No statistically significant sex-associated differences were detected. Tri-BBPA was undetectable or negligible across incubations. Notably, the cumulative sulfatase-maturation enzyme gene family abundance was positively associated with LC-MS-measured S-TBBPA deconjugation activity, whereas the cumulative arylsulfatase and other sulfatase gene abundances showed no significant associations. Furthermore, 12 taxonomically stratified microbial desulfation-related gene-family annotations exhibited nominally significant positive correlations with deconjugation activity, highlighting potential roles for specific microbial sulfatases and their maturation enzymes in TBBPA reactivation. Collectively, our PM10 pilot study revealed substantial interindividual variability in microbial TBBPA-sulfate deconjugation and identified sulfatase-maturation enzyme gene abundance as a potential indicator of activity. These findings highlighted an underexplored pathway of xenobiotic reactivation and support future personalized microbiome-directed strategies to reduce internal TBBPA exposure and associated health risks.

papers.title: Benchmarking honorific academic recognitions against citation metrics
papers.abstract: We examined how diverse metrics track individuals receiving major honorific recognitions and whether higher, more prestigious recognitions are associated with higher coverage among a database of top-cited scientists. We assessed with Scopus data the newly inducted (in 2026) 2,038 members of 14 major academies and honorific societies, endowed professors at Stanford University (n=773) and Michigan State University (MSU) endowed professors (n=129) and distinguished professors (n=112), and Nobel (n=166) and Turing (n=25) laureates awarded in 2010-2026 (n=191) for total publications, total citations, h-index, coauthorship-adjusted hm-index, citations to single-, single/first-, and single-/first-/last-authored (SFL) publications, and a composite citation indicator (c-score). For those with [≥]5 full papers and [≥]20 published items indexed in Scopus, metrics were mapped as percentile values among authors sharing the same primary scientific subfield and [≥]5 full papers. Citations to SFL publications had most frequently the best median percentile values and c-score had the best median of median percentile values (0.81%). Subfield-adjusted median percentile values were 0.04-0.23% for Turing/Nobel, 0.23-3.01% for academies and honorific societies, 2.74% for MSU endowed professors, 1.29% for MSU distinguished professors, 0.94% for Stanford endowed professors for citations to SFL publications; and 0.04-0.26%, 0.36-3.85%, 3.21%, 1.55%, 1.03%, respectively, for c-score. The percentages of honorees included in the Stanford/Elsevier listing of top-cited scientists (top-2% of c-score in their scientific subfield or top-100,000 in c-score across all science) followed the perceived prestige gradient: 99% for Turing/Nobel laureates, 84-92% for the national US academies and the UK Royal Society as well as AAP and ACM, 51-76% for other academies/societies, 78% for Stanford endowed professorships, 72% for distinguished MSU professorships, 52% for MSU endowed professorships. Several honored scientists had at least one retraction (highest for medicine (17.5%) and chemistry (11.4%) Nobel laureates), and few had very high proportion of papers in Scopus-discontinued titles, while high self-citations were rarely encountered. Metrics may influence honors and vice versa. The current evidence suggests strong tracking of the median values, especially for citations to SFL publications and c-score, against major recognitions; and a gradient of coverage in a list of top-cited scientists congruent with the perceived relative prestige of these recognitions.

papers.title: Visual Landmarks Influence Eye-Hand Coordination in Memory-Guided Reaches
papers.abstract: The human visual system optimally weighs egocentric cues (e.g., object location relative to the eye) and allocentric cues (e.g., object location relative to other landmarks) to aim actions. The neural mechanisms of this process have been studied in the primate gaze system, but it is not known how these results extend to eye-hand coordination and the reach system. Here, reach and gaze (eye-in-space) data were collected from two head-unrestrained Macaca mulatta (M1, M2) trained to reach toward remembered visual targets on a touch screen. During the delay, animals either saw nothing (no-landmark), a pattern of 'dots' around the target (stable landmark), or a similar landmark that reappeared at a shifted position (landmark shift). In most conditions, increased delay times (up to 1200 ms) reduced reaction times, with minimal effects on gaze and reach errors. In the temporal domain, landmarks reduced gaze reaction time, increased the time to final hand touch, and reduced gaze-hand coupling. In the spatial domain, the stable landmark tended to improve reach accuracy and precision but reduced landmark-centered gaze-hand coupling. Landmark shifts increased errors in pooled datasets, due to weighted (and modestly correlated) shifts in both reach and gaze in the same direction. The 'allocentric weights' for reach were also modulated by initial gaze position. Overall, these data suggest that visual landmarks influence the timing, accuracy, and coordination of gaze / hand movements, likely through visual feedback during reach, and these effectors share a similar mechanism for optimal integration of egocentric and allocentric visual cues.

papers.title: Multimodal private information and reward value shape information use during ant foraging
papers.abstract: Animals use both private information acquired through experience and social information produced by conspecifics when making behavioural decisions. The combination of sensory cues and their associated reward value may influence how animals weigh private information against social information. We investigated information use during foraging in the ant Pristomyrmex punctatus using Y-maze experiments with learned visual and olfactory cues and trail pheromones. Workers learned both types of private cue and showed no significant preference between them when they were placed in conflict. When private information conflicted with a high-concentration pheromone trail, workers preferred the pheromone-marked route following visual, olfactory or multimodal training. At a lower pheromone concentration, route choice depended on training modality: workers trained with either unimodal cue preferred the pheromone trail, whereas workers trained with multimodal cues (combined visual and olfactory cues) showed no significant preference between the routes. When learned visual and olfactory cues were placed in conflict, workers favoured the cue paired with the higher sucrose concentration under both reciprocal reward assignments. In contrast, workers still preferred a pheromone trail when it had been associated with a lower-quality reward than the competing multimodal cues. These results show that ants adjust their use of learned private information according to expected reward and suggest that multimodal private information can influence the balance between private and social information during foraging.

papers.title: Quantitative analysis of HDAC inhibition using the TGx-HDACi transcriptomic biomarker in human TK6 cells
papers.abstract: Transcriptomic biomarkers provide an objective approach for extracting mechanistic information from complex gene expression datasets and may support quantitative applications in chemical assessment. TGx-HDACi is an 81-gene transcriptomic biomarker designed to identify histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) in human TK6 cells. We evaluated whether benchmark concentrations (BMCs) derived from TGx-HDACi responses are concordant with BMCs based on reductions in HDAC enzyme activity. Human TK6 cells were exposed to concentration ranges of three HDAC inhibitors from different representative classes: the pan-HDAC inhibitors trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), and the class I-selective inhibitor entinostat. HDAC enzyme activity and TGx-HDACi responses were assessed, and concentration-response modeling was performed to derive BMCs. TGx-HDACi correctly identified all three compounds as HDAC inhibitors and showed concentration-dependent responses. For TSA and VPA, TGx-HDACi and HDAC activity BMCs had overlapping confidence intervals, indicating good agreement between potency measures. In contrast, entinostat produced higher TGx-HDACi BMCs than the enzyme assay. This reduced quantitative concordance may reflect differences in HDAC selectivity, as TGx-HDACi was developed primarily using pan-HDAC inhibitors and appears less responsive to the more limited transcriptional changes induced by class I-selective inhibitors. Overall, these results demonstrate that TGx-HDACi reliably identifies HDAC inhibition and can provide potency estimates that align with enzyme activity measures for some HDAC inhibitor classes. However, the findings highlight the importance of considering biomarker applicability domain when interpreting potency estimates across compounds with differing HDAC selectivity.

papers.title: Long-Acting GLP-1 Receptor Agonism Ameliorates Sinoatrial Node Dysfunction by Attenuating Electrophysiological and Structural Remodeling
papers.abstract: Background: Sinoatrial node dysfunction (SND) causes bradyarrhythmia, while pacemaker therapy does not reverse injury to the sinoatrial node (SAN). Long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) raise heart rate, but whether they can repair an injured SAN in SND remains unknown. Methods: In streptozotocin-induced SND rats, we studied an acute phase (SND, GLP-1RA treatment, glycemic control, and GLP-1R antagonist groups) and a chronic phase (SND, GLP-1RA treatment, and glycemic control groups). Endpoints included heart rate, RR interval, heart rate variability, intrinsic heart rate (IHR), corrected sinus node recovery time after adenosine injection (ADSNRT), SAN transcriptomics, histology and immunofluorescence, HL-1 cell oxidative-stress studies, and public single-cell data. Results: At the acute endpoint, the long-acting GLP-1RA efsubaglutide alfa (eSuba) increased heart rate (372.76 {+/-} 11.06 vs 312.64 {+/-} 22.28 beats/min; P < 0.0001) and IHR (349.45 {+/-} 10.49 vs 234.79 {+/-} 12.29 beats/min; P < 0.0001), and shortened ADSNRT (4.22 {+/-} 2.75 vs 20.68 {+/-} 1.60 s; P = 0.0009); improvements in heart rate (349.05 {+/-} 17.73 vs 266.02 {+/-} 13.52 beats/min; P < 0.0001) and IHR persisted in the chronic phase. SAN transcriptomics showed reversal of extracellular matrix, inflammatory/immune, redox/mitochondrial, glial, and electrical programs. The GLP-1RA reduced collagen deposition and CCR2a+ infiltration, decreased ox-CaMKII/CaMKII, increased SIRT3, restored Cav1.3, Nav1.5, SERCA2a and p-RyR2 (Ser2808), and increased p-PKA/PKA. The glycemic control comparator produced limited improvement, and the GLP-1R antagonist attenuated most effects. Conclusions: Long-acting GLP-1R agonism improves SAN function in SND via glucose-independent attenuation of electrophysiological and structural remodeling, an effect that is at least partly GLP-1R dependent.

papers.title: Neuroprotective Effects of the Purine-Derived Compound ITH15004 Against Nigericin- and Mitochondria-Induced Toxicity in NSC-34 Motor Neuron-like Cells
authors: P. K. de Moraes Berenguel Lossavaro
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive degeneration of motor neurons. Most patients die within 3 to 5 years of diagnosis, primarily due to respiratory failure, and effective therapeutic options remain limited. Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, calcium dysregulation, and neuroinflammation are key contributors to ALS pathogenesis. In this study, we evaluated the potential neuroprotective effects of ITH15004, a novel compound with modulatory effects on P2X7 purinergic receptors, in an in vitro model using NSC-34 motor neuron-like cells. Cellular stress was induced using oligomycin (10 uM) and rotenone (30 uM), inhibitors of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation; nigericin (5 uM), a K+/H+ ionophore that disrupts ionic homeostasis; and extracellular ATP (1 mM), a purinergic receptor agonist. MTT-reducing activity was assessed as an indicator of cellular metabolic activity, while caspase-3/7 activity was measured to evaluate apoptotic responses. Intracellular ATP levels, cytosolic calcium responses, and cytochrome c and VDAC1 protein abundance were also analysed. ITH15004 significantly improved MTT-reducing activity following exposure to ATP, oligomycin/rotenone, and nigericin. In addition, ITH15004 partially restored intracellular ATP levels following nigericin treatment and significantly reduced nigericin-induced caspase-3/7 activation. Western blot analysis further revealed significant changes in cytochrome c and VDAC1 protein levels in response to ITH15004 treatment. These findings indicate that ITH15004 attenuates cellular damage induced by different stressors in NSC-34 cells and modulates several parameters associated with cellular energy status and apoptotic signalling. Further studies are needed to establish its mechanisms of action and assess its therapeutic potential in ALS.

papers.title: Cardiomyocytes in Persistent Cancer Therapy-related Cardiac Dysfunction Show Contractile and Natriuretic Peptide Signaling Signatures
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND. Anthracycline and trastuzumab therapy of HER2-positive breast cancer causes cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) in a subset of treated patients. Some recover cardiac function, others do not. Whether persistence is a cardiomyocyte-intrinsic property is unknown. OBJECTIVES. We sought to determine whether induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from patients with persistent CTRCD respond to these drugs differently from those of patients with reversible or no CTRCD, and to identify the functional pathways involved. METHODS. iPSCs were derived from 23 women with normal baseline cardiac function treated with doxorubicin-based chemotherapy followed by trastuzumab: 5, 11 and 7 with no, reversible, and persistent CTRCD, respectively. iPSC-CMs were exposed to 7 drug regimens, generating 161 transcriptomic profiles that we resolved by singular value decomposition and subjected to pathway enrichment analysis. Reliability was tested by 100 clinical label permutations and leave-one-patient-out downsampling. RESULTS. Persistent CTRCD responses clustered more tightly and separated from reversible and no-CTRCD responses to a higher degree than expected by chance (P = 0.04). Reversible and no-CTRCD responses did not resolve from one another. Genes encoding guideline-recommended biomarkers, including natriuretic peptides and cardiac troponins, were more strongly induced or less repressed in persistent CTRCD cell lines, while natriuretic peptide receptor signaling was lower. Contraction, calcium handling, cytoskeletal and glycolytic pathways differed between CTRCD groups. Comparison with signatures induced by cardiotoxic kinase inhibitors in healthy donor cardiomyocytes documented high functional similarities. CONCLUSIONS. Cardiomyocytes display a cell-intrinsic signature of persistent CTRCD that centers on contractile homeostasis and natriuretic peptide receptor signaling, supporting patient group-selective cardioprotective intervention strategies.
